# EBS and instance store: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q014 -->
### Question 1

A company runs a PostgreSQL database on one Amazon EC2 instance. The database uses a 2 TiB General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS data volume, but the volume holds only 200 GiB of data, and the data grows slowly. The company wants to cut the monthly storage cost of this volume. The database team accepts a short maintenance window. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Modify the existing volume to 300 GiB with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and then shrink the partition and the file system.
- Create a snapshot of the volume, restore the snapshot into a new 300 GiB gp3 volume, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.
- Create a new 300 GiB gp3 volume, copy the data to it with a file copy tool, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.
- Create a new 1 TiB gp3 volume, copy the data to it with a file copy tool, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a new 300 GiB gp3 volume, copy the data to it with a file copy tool, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.

**Deciding phrases.** "2 TiB", "holds only 200 GiB of data", "grows slowly", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective way to cut the storage cost of one volume.
2. I mark the constraints: a 2 TiB gp3 volume, 200 GiB of slowly growing data, a database, and a short maintenance window that the team accepts.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict Elastic Volumes: I modify the volume to a smaller size while the database runs.
4. I remove the new 1 TiB volume, because it still pays for far more storage than the data needs. I remove the snapshot restore, because a volume from a snapshot is equal to or larger than the snapshot's volume size.
5. Between the Elastic Volumes change and the copy to a new 300 GiB volume the difference is direction. My first idea breaks because you can't decrease the volume size with Elastic Volumes; AWS says to create a smaller volume and copy the data, and the maintenance window allows that.
6. Check: the new 300 GiB gp3 volume holds the data with room to grow, and deleting the old volume ends its charge. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Storage is [charged by the amount of GB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month) that you provision, so the cost follows the 2 TiB, not the 200 GiB of data. Elastic Volumes does not help here, because [you can't decrease the volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease). The way down is a new, smaller volume, a copy of the data in the maintenance window, and the deletion of the old volume.

**Why not.**

- "Modify the existing volume to 300 GiB with ...": Elastic Volumes can grow a volume, but [you can't decrease the volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease), so the change to a smaller size fails.
- "Create a snapshot of the volume, restore the ...": A volume restored from a snapshot must be [equal to or larger than](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-from-snapshot-size-at-least-source) the snapshot's volume size, so a restore cannot make it smaller.
- "Create a new 1 TiB gp3 volume, copy ...": It works, but storage is [charged by the amount of GB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month) that you provision, and that size is far more than the slowly growing data needs.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the volume is nearly full and the data keeps growing" instead: increase the size with Elastic Volumes, [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).

**Takeaway.** An EBS volume grows in place but does not shrink; to shrink, copy the data to a smaller new volume.

**Review.** [Elastic Volumes grows or retunes a volume in place but cannot shrink it](2-deep.md#elastic-volumes-grows-or-retunes-a-volume-in-place-but-cannot-shrink-it-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs a MySQL database on one Amazon EC2 instance. The database stores its data on a 100 GiB General Purpose SSD (gp2) Amazon EBS volume. After a product launch, the database needs 8,000 IOPS, but the volume does not deliver that many IOPS. The data will stay near 100 GiB for the next year. The change must cause minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Increase the size of the gp2 volume with Elastic Volumes until its baseline performance reaches 8,000 IOPS, and keep the gp2 volume type.
- Attach more gp2 volumes, build a RAID 0 array across all of them, and move the database files to the array to add their IOPS.
- Change the volume type to gp3 with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and provision 8,000 IOPS on the same 100 GiB volume.
- Change the volume type to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and provision 8,000 IOPS.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Change the volume type to gp3 with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and provision 8,000 IOPS on the same 100 GiB volume.

**Deciding phrases.** "100 GiB General Purpose SSD (gp2)", "needs 8,000 IOPS", "stay near 100 GiB", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution.
2. I mark the constraints: a 100 GiB gp2 volume, 8,000 IOPS needed, data that stays near 100 GiB, and minimal downtime.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict gp3, because gp3 provisions IOPS independently of volume size, and Elastic Volumes changes the type while the instance runs.
4. I remove the RAID 0 array, because it adds volumes and a move of the database files, which means more storage and downtime. I remove the larger gp2 volume, because gp2 gives 3 IOPS per GiB, so 8,000 IOPS needs many times the storage that the data uses.
5. Between gp3 and io2 Block Express the difference is what the higher price buys: higher durability, better latency consistency and more performance than gp3 gives; the stem asks for none of these, so gp3 is enough.
6. Check: gp3 with 8,000 IOPS keeps 100 GiB, changes in place and is the lowest cost SSD volume type. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** gp3 separates size and speed: you provision IOPS [without needing to provision additional block storage capacity](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), so the volume stays at 100 GiB. Elastic Volumes makes the change while the database runs. gp3 is also [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd) type, so the company pays for no extra storage and no premium volume type.

**Why not.**

- "Increase the size of the gp2 volume with ...": It works, but gp2 baseline IOPS grow at [3 IOPS per GiB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp2-iops-per-gib), so the company pays for many times the storage that the data needs.
- "Attach more gp2 volumes, build a RAID 0 ...": [Creating a RAID 0 array](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume) adds the IOPS of each volume, but the extra volumes add storage, and moving the database files adds downtime.
- "Change the volume type to Provisioned IOPS SSD ...": It works, but AWS recommends io2 Block Express for [higher durability, better latency consistency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when) or more than gp3 gives, and the stem asks for neither.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database also needs consistent sub-millisecond latency" instead: io2 Block Express, because it serves workloads that need [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases).

**Takeaway.** More IOPS without more space: change gp2 to gp3 in place and provision the IOPS.

**Review.** [gp3 lets you buy IOPS and throughput without buying more storage](2-deep.md#gp3-lets-you-buy-iops-and-throughput-without-buying-more-storage-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs a workload on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The instance boots from a separate root volume, and the workload keeps its data on one 2 TiB Amazon EBS data volume. The workload is a relational database with small, random reads and writes that needs about 10,000 IOPS. The company must choose the volume type for the data volume. Which volume type is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?

- A General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, with IOPS and throughput provisioned above the included baseline only as far as the workload needs them.
- A Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, with IOPS provisioned for the busiest hour of the workload and kept at that level all day.
- A Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume, sized so that its throughput matches the reads and writes that the workload performs each day.
- A Cold HDD (sc1) volume, which has the lowest storage price per GB of all EBS volume types, sized to hold the data of the workload.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** A General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, with IOPS and throughput provisioned above the included baseline only as far as the workload needs them.

**Deciding phrases.** "relational database with small, random reads and writes", "about 10,000 IOPS", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Small, random reads and writes at about 10,000 IOPS decide this question. SSD volumes serve [transactional, IOPS-intensive database workloads, boot volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-ssd-workloads), and HDD volumes do not. Among the SSD types, gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd), and you provision its IOPS [independently of volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), so the database gets its IOPS without the price of io2 Block Express.

**Why not.**

- "A Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, ...": It works, but it costs more; AWS points to io2 Block Express for [higher durability, better latency consistency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when) or more IOPS than gp3, and the stem asks for none of these.
- "A Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume, sized so ...": A transactional workload with small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), so st1 fails the 10,000 IOPS need of the database.
- "A Cold HDD (sc1) volume, which has the ...": The lowest price does not help when the volume fails the need: sc1 fits [colder data requiring fewer scans per day](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-sc1-use-cases), not small, random database I/O.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a log processing job that reads large files sequentially many times a day and must finish each scan quickly" instead: st1, which fits [big data, data warehouses, log processing](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-st1-use-cases).

**Takeaway.** Small, random database I/O at a moderate IOPS level points to gp3, the lowest-cost SSD type.

**Review.** [SSD volumes serve small random IO and HDD volumes serve large sequential reads](2-deep.md#ssd-volumes-serve-small-random-io-and-hdd-volumes-serve-large-sequential-reads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that stores its data on one Amazon EBS volume. The company accepts the loss of up to one day of data and a recovery time of several hours. The company does not run any of its instances across multiple Availability Zones today. The company must be able to recover the database if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the same Region.
- Take a daily snapshot of the volume and copy it to a second Region. After a failure, create a volume from the copy there.
- Keep the data on the current volume. After a failure, detach the volume and attach it to a new instance in another Availability Zone of the Region.
- Take a daily snapshot and copy it to a second Region. Keep a standby instance running there, and restore each new copy to its volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the same Region.

**Deciding phrases.** "if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable", "loss of up to one day of data", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The loss of one zone, with one day of data loss allowed, decides this question. Snapshot data is [replicated across all Availability Zones in the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region), so you can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region) of that Region after the zone fails. A daily snapshot meets the one-day limit, and the company pays for no copy in a second Region and no running standby.

**Why not.**

- "Take a daily snapshot of the volume and ...": It works, but a copy is [charged for the data transferred across regions](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-charge) and stored twice, and the loss of one zone does not need a second Region.
- "Keep the data on the current volume. After ...": The volume and the instance [must be in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance), so the volume in the failed zone cannot be attached to an instance in another zone.
- "Take a daily snapshot and copy it to ...": It works, but a standby instance that runs every day and a copy in a second Region cost more, and the company accepts several hours of recovery.

**Twin.** If the stem said "if the whole Region becomes unavailable" instead: copy each snapshot to a second Region, because [snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing) where they are created.

**Takeaway.** The loss of a zone needs a snapshot restored in another zone; the loss of a Region needs a copy in another Region.

**Review.** [A restored volume can start in any zone but reads slowly at first](2-deep.md#a-restored-volume-can-start-in-any-zone-but-reads-slowly-at-first-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs a media processing application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. Each instance writes many working files while it processes a job, and the job needs fast performance for small, random reads and writes. The files are temporary scratch data that the application can re-create from Amazon S3, and the storage must give the lowest latency possible. Which storage solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Launch the fleet on an instance type that provides instance store volumes, and write the working files to those volumes.
- Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
- Create one Amazon EFS file system, mount it on every instance in the fleet, and write the working files to it.
- Attach a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch the fleet on an instance type that provides instance store volumes, and write the working files to those volumes.

**Deciding phrases.** "temporary scratch data", "can re-create from Amazon S3", "the lowest latency possible", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Instance store is [temporary block-level storage](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-physically-attached-host-disks) on disks of the host computer, and [there is no additional charge](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-no-additional-charge) for it. Its data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop). That loss costs nothing here, because the application can re-create the files from Amazon S3.

**Why not.**

- "Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS ...": It works, but each volume is [charged by the amount of GB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month) that you provision, and average EBS latency is [single-digit milliseconds](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-average-latency) for files that the job can re-create.
- "Create one Amazon EFS file system, mount it ...": Amazon EFS is for [shared read and write access across multiple Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-decision-guide-file-storage-shared-access), but each instance here works on its own scratch files.
- "Attach a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume ...": Small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), so the job loses the fast reads and writes that it needs.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the files must still be there after a weekly stop and start" instead: a gp3 volume on each instance, because it [remains attached throughout the stop-start cycle](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start).

**Takeaway.** Scratch data that can be re-created and needs the lowest latency goes on instance store, not on EBS.

**Review.** [Instance store data lives on the host and ends with the instance](2-deep.md#instance-store-data-lives-on-the-host-and-ends-with-the-instance-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q008 -->
### Question 6

A company launches Amazon EC2 instances from a launch template. Each instance has one Amazon EBS root volume, and the template keeps the default settings for that volume. When the company terminates an instance, the root volume disappears. An auditor now requires the company to retain the data of each root volume after its instance is terminated. What should the company change in the launch template for future launches?

- Make no change, because Amazon EBS volumes persist after their instance is terminated, whatever the settings are.
- Add an instance store volume to the template, and copy the root volume data to it before each termination.
- Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume to true in the block device mapping of the template.
- Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume to false in the block device mapping of the template.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume to false in the block device mapping of the template.

**Deciding phrases.** "keeps the default settings", "the root volume disappears", "retain the data of each root volume"

**Why.** Each EBS volume has a [DeleteOnTermination](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-delete-on-termination-defaults) attribute, and [the default is to delete the root volume](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-delete-on-termination-defaults) when the instance terminates. To keep a root volume, AWS says to set its [Delete on termination flag](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-root-delete-on-termination-no) to No, which is false in the block device mapping of the template.

**Why not.**

- "Make no change, because Amazon EBS volumes persist ...": The root volume created at launch is [deleted when that instance is terminated](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true) while its flag keeps the default.
- "Add an instance store volume to the template, ...": Instance store data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), so the copy disappears with the instance.
- "Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume ...": A true flag deletes the volume at termination, which is the behavior the company has now, because [the default is to delete the root volume](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-delete-on-termination-defaults).

**Twin.** If the stem said "retain a second data volume that was created at launch" instead: no change is needed, because other volumes created at launch [are not deleted when that instance is terminated](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-delete-on-termination-additional-default-false).

**Takeaway.** The root volume is deleted at termination unless DeleteOnTermination is false.

**Review.** [An EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone and can outlive its instance](2-deep.md#an-ebs-volume-lives-in-one-availability-zone-and-can-outlive-its-instance-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs an application on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The application writes its data to a 500 GiB gp3 Amazon EBS data volume, and the volume is almost full. The data grows by about 20 GiB each week. The application cannot be stopped, so the team must add storage without downtime. Which action should the team take to meet these requirements?

- Stop the instance, detach the volume, and attach a new, larger gp3 volume that holds a copy of the data.
- Increase the size of the volume with Elastic Volumes, and then extend the partition and the file system inside the instance.
- Create a snapshot of the volume, restore the snapshot to a larger gp3 volume, and switch the application to the restored volume.
- Attach an instance store volume to the running instance, and move the oldest data of the application to that volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Increase the size of the volume with Elastic Volumes, and then extend the partition and the file system inside the instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "without downtime", "the volume is almost full"

**Why.** The words "without downtime" decide this question. With Elastic Volumes you can increase the size of a volume [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach). The new size can be used after the modification [reaches the optimizing state](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-modification-size-effective-at-optimizing), and then you extend the partition and the file system.

**Why not.**

- "Stop the instance, detach the volume, and attach ...": Stopping the instance is downtime, and Elastic Volumes grows a volume [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).
- "Create a snapshot of the volume, restore the ...": The switch interrupts the application, and a restored volume is slow at first because its blocks are [downloaded from Amazon S3 to the new volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot).
- "Attach an instance store volume to the running ...": You can attach instance store volumes to an instance [only when you launch it](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-attach-only-at-launch), so the running instance cannot get one.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the volume has free space, but the database needs more IOPS" instead: provision more IOPS on the gp3 volume, again [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).

**Takeaway.** More space with no downtime means Elastic Volumes, then a larger partition and file system.

**Review.** [Elastic Volumes grows or retunes a volume in place but cannot shrink it](2-deep.md#elastic-volumes-grows-or-retunes-a-volume-in-place-but-cannot-shrink-it-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs a media processing application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. Each instance writes many working files while it processes a job, and the job needs about 2,000 IOPS of small, random reads and writes on each instance. The company must make sure that the files are still there after the instances are stopped and started again for maintenance every weekend. Which storage solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Launch the fleet on an instance type that provides instance store volumes, and write the working files to those volumes.
- Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
- Attach a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
- Attach a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.

**Deciding phrases.** "still there after the instances are stopped and started again", "about 2,000 IOPS of small, random reads and writes", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is the weekend stop and start. An EBS volume is [off-instance storage](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-persists-independently-of-instance) that [remains attached throughout the stop-start cycle](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start), while instance store data is [cryptographically erased](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop) at a stop. Among the EBS types, gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd), and its included [3,000 IOPS](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-baseline-iops) cover the 2,000 IOPS of each instance.

**Why not.**

- "Launch the fleet on an instance type that ...": Instance store data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), so the weekend stop erases the files.
- "Attach a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) ...": It works, but io2 Block Express is for needs such as [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), while gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd).
- "Attach a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume ...": Small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), so a low price per GB does not help when the job needs fast I/O.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the files are temporary scratch data that need the lowest latency" instead: instance store, because it gives [high random I/O performance with very low latency](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-ssd-high-random-io).

**Takeaway.** Data that has to survive a stop goes on an EBS volume, not on instance store.

**Review.** [Instance store data lives on the host and ends with the instance](2-deep.md#instance-store-data-lives-on-the-host-and-ends-with-the-instance-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs an application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The application keeps its data on an unencrypted Amazon EBS data volume. A new security policy requires the company to encrypt this data at rest. The company must also ensure that every new EBS volume that anyone creates in the Region from now on is encrypted. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Create a snapshot of the volume, copy the snapshot with encryption turned on, and replace the volume with a new volume from the copy.
- Use Elastic Volumes to modify the existing volume in place, and turn on encryption while the volume stays attached to the running instance of the application.
- Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and wait for Amazon EBS to encrypt the existing volume in the background.
- Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and keep the AWS managed key as the default encryption key.
- Create an AWS Lambda function that runs every hour, finds new unencrypted volumes in the Region, and replaces each one with an encrypted copy.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a snapshot of the volume, copy the snapshot with encryption turned on, and replace the volume with a new volume from the copy.
- Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and keep the AWS managed key as the default encryption key.

**Deciding phrases.** "unencrypted Amazon EBS data volume", "every new EBS volume", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two needs decide this question: the existing data and every new volume. The existing data moves to an encrypted volume through an encrypted snapshot copy. Encryption by default then makes the account [enforce the encryption of the new EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only), with one Region setting and no code.

- [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), so you snapshot the volume and [create an encrypted copy of that snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot) for a new volume.
- Encryption by default is a [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region), and it ensures that [all new volumes are always encrypted](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) there.

**Why not.**

- "Use Elastic Volumes to modify the existing volume ...": You [cannot change the encryption status](../facts/kms.md#kms-ebs-encryption-status-fixed-at-create) of an existing volume, so Elastic Volumes offers no setting that encrypts it in place.
- "Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in ...": Encryption by default [has no effect on existing EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only), so the existing volume stays unencrypted.
- "Create an AWS Lambda function that runs every ...": A scheduled function is code to build and run, and a new volume stays unencrypted until the next run; one [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) covers every new volume.

**Twin.** If the stem said "every new volume in two Regions" instead: turn on encryption by default in each Region, because it is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting).

**Takeaway.** Encrypt an existing volume through an encrypted snapshot copy; for new volumes, use the [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region).

**Review.** [EBS encryption covers the volume its snapshots and the path to the instance](2-deep.md#ebs-encryption-covers-the-volume-its-snapshots-and-the-path-to-the-instance-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q012 -->
### Question 10

A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that stores its data on one Amazon EBS volume. The company accepts the loss of up to one day of data and a recovery time of several hours. The company does not run any of its instances across multiple Availability Zones today. The company must be able to recover the database if the whole Region becomes unavailable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the same Region.
- Take a daily snapshot of the volume and copy it to a second Region. After a failure, create a volume from the copy there.
- Keep the data on the current volume. After a failure, detach the volume and attach it to a new instance in another Availability Zone of the Region.
- Take a daily snapshot and copy it to a second Region. Keep a standby instance running there, and restore each new copy to its volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Take a daily snapshot of the volume and copy it to a second Region. After a failure, create a volume from the copy there.

**Deciding phrases.** "if the whole Region becomes unavailable", "loss of up to one day of data", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The loss of the whole Region, with one day of data loss allowed, decides this question. [Snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing) where they are created, so a backup that must outlive the Region needs a copy in a second Region. You can [copy snapshots from one Region to another](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt) each day and restore the latest copy after a failure.

**Why not.**

- "Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After ...": A restore in another zone stays in the same Region, because [snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing), and that whole Region is down.
- "Keep the data on the current volume. After ...": The volume and the instance [must be in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance), and the whole Region is down, so the volume cannot be attached anywhere.
- "Take a daily snapshot and copy it to ...": It works, but a standby instance that runs every day costs more than a restore after a failure, and several hours of recovery are acceptable.

**Twin.** If the stem said "if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable" instead: restore the latest snapshot in another zone, because you can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region) of the Region.

**Takeaway.** A backup that has to outlive a Region needs a snapshot copy in a second Region.

**Review.** [Copying or sharing a snapshot puts the backup in another Region or account](2-deep.md#copying-or-sharing-a-snapshot-puts-the-backup-in-another-region-or-account-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q016 -->
### Question 11

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Users upload images, and every instance must read and write the same set of image files with standard file operations. The solution must keep working if one Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create one Amazon EFS file system, and configure every instance to mount it at startup in each Availability Zone.
- Create one Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with Multi-Attach enabled, and attach the volume to every instance in each Availability Zone.
- Attach a gp3 volume to each instance, and run a scheduled job on every instance that copies new image files to the other instances.
- Use the instance store volumes of each instance, and run a scheduled job on every instance that copies new image files to the other instances.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create one Amazon EFS file system, and configure every instance to mount it at startup in each Availability Zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "across multiple Availability Zones", "every instance must read and write the same set of image files", "keep working if one Availability Zone fails", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Every instance, in several zones, reads and writes the same files, so the need is shared file storage. Amazon EFS is a [file storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object) that stores data [within and across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing). An EBS volume is [automatically replicated within its Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-replicated-within-az), so a volume belongs to one zone.

**Why not.**

- "Create one Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with ...": Multi-Attach works for instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), and with several writers you [use a clustered file system](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system), not standard file operations.
- "Attach a gp3 volume to each instance, and ...": It works, but the team builds and runs a copy job on every instance, which is more work than one shared file system.
- "Use the instance store volumes of each instance, ...": Instance store data is lost when an instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), and Auto Scaling terminates instances, so uploaded images can disappear.

**Twin.** If the stem said "two cluster nodes in one Availability Zone share one block device" instead: an io2 volume with Multi-Attach, which can [attach a single Provisioned IOPS SSD](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) volume to several instances.

**Takeaway.** Shared files across Availability Zones point to Amazon EFS; an EBS volume stays in one zone.

**Review.** [Multi-Attach shares one io2 volume and the application must coordinate writes](2-deep.md#multi-attach-shares-one-io2-volume-and-the-application-must-coordinate-writes-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q020 -->
### Question 12

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that store data on Amazon EBS volumes in one AWS Region. The company must back up the volumes every day and keep each backup for 30 days. Operators sometimes delete snapshots by mistake, and the company must be able to recover a snapshot that was deleted in the last week. The company wants to automate the solution. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Rely on the replication that Amazon EBS performs for every volume, because it already keeps extra copies of the data for recovery.
- Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that targets the volumes by tag, takes a snapshot every day, and keeps each snapshot for 30 days.
- Run a cron job on each instance that calls the AWS CLI every day to create snapshots and to delete the snapshots that are older than 30 days.
- Change the volumes to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volumes, because their higher durability removes the need for daily snapshots.
- Create a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots in the Region, with a retention period that keeps deleted snapshots for at least 7 days.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that targets the volumes by tag, takes a snapshot every day, and keeps each snapshot for 30 days.
- Create a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots in the Region, with a retention period that keeps deleted snapshots for at least 7 days.

**Deciding phrases.** "back up the volumes every day", "delete snapshots by mistake", "recover a snapshot that was deleted", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS [does not automatically back up the data](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-no-automatic-backup-customer-creates-snapshots), so a Data Lifecycle Manager policy takes the daily snapshots and deletes them after 30 days. A deletion by mistake needs a second guard: a deleted snapshot that matches a retention rule is [retained in the Recycle Bin](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-delete-retained-by-recycle-bin-rule) and can be restored.

- A policy automates the [creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis) and keeps them by [either their total count or their age](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type).
- Recycle Bin protects snapshots after you create rules [in the AWS Regions in which you want](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-recycle-bin-needs-regional-retention-rules) protection, and you restore [at any time before its retention period expires](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-recycle-bin-expired-permanently-deleted).

**Why not.**

- "Rely on the replication that Amazon EBS performs ...": Replication protects against the [failure of any single hardware component](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-replicated-within-az), not against a deleted snapshot or a lost zone.
- "Run a cron job on each instance that ...": It works, but the team writes and maintains a script on every instance, while a policy does the job [at no additional cost](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis).
- "Change the volumes to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 ...": Durability, snapshots and copies in other zones [protect against different types of failures](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-io2-still-snapshot-and-replicate), so durability is no backup.

**Twin.** If the stem said "one policy must cover Amazon EBS, Amazon RDS and Amazon EFS across accounts" instead: AWS Backup, because you [apply it across accounts and Regions](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-aws-backup-central-policy-across-accounts).

**Takeaway.** Schedule snapshots with Data Lifecycle Manager, and undo deletions with a Recycle Bin rule in each Region.

**Review.** [Data Lifecycle Manager and AWS Backup take snapshots on a schedule](2-deep.md#data-lifecycle-manager-and-aws-backup-take-snapshots-on-a-schedule-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q005 -->
### Question 13

A company runs a mission-critical database on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The database makes small, random reads and writes and needs about 12,000 IOPS. It needs low latency: the storage must give consistent sub-millisecond latency. The data volume must also have the highest durability that Amazon EBS offers. Which storage configuration is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?

- Use one General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, and provision 12,000 IOPS and the throughput that the database needs above the included baseline.
- Use one Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume that is large enough to give the database high throughput for its reads and writes.
- Use two Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volumes in a RAID 1 mirror, and provision 12,000 IOPS on each volume.
- Use one Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, and provision the 12,000 IOPS that the database needs on that volume.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use one Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, and provision the 12,000 IOPS that the database needs on that volume.

**Deciding phrases.** "consistent sub-millisecond latency", "the highest durability that Amazon EBS offers", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Sub-millisecond latency and the highest EBS durability decide this question. io2 Block Express is the EBS type for [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), and it offers [100X greater durability](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-io2-durability-99999) than other EBS volumes. One volume with the needed IOPS meets both requirements, so a mirror adds cost and meets no extra requirement.

**Why not.**

- "Use one General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, and ...": gp3 gives [single-digit millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-latency) and is designed for [99.8 percent to 99.9 percent](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-durability-afr) durability, so it fails both storage requirements.
- "Use one Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume that ...": A database with small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), and st1 fails the latency need as well.
- "Use two Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) ...": It meets the needs, but two volumes double the cost, and AWS says [RAID 1 is also not recommended](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-raid1-not-recommended) for EBS volumes.

**Twin.** If the stem said "single-digit millisecond latency and normal EBS durability are acceptable" instead: one gp3 volume with provisioned IOPS, for a [balance between cost and performance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-suited-workloads).

**Takeaway.** Sub-millisecond latency or the highest EBS durability points to one io2 Block Express volume.

**Review.** [io2 Block Express buys more IOPS lower latency and higher durability](2-deep.md#io2-block-express-buys-more-iops-lower-latency-and-higher-durability-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q015 -->
### Question 14

A company runs an application on two Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are built on the Nitro System. Both instances are in the same Availability Zone. The application must be highly available, so both nodes must read and write the same block storage at the same time, and either node must be able to take over at once. The application itself does not coordinate writes between the two nodes. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Create a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to both instances.
- Create a General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to both instances in the zone.
- Format the shared volume with the XFS file system, and mount the file system on both instances at the same time.
- Format the shared volume with a clustered file system, and let the cluster software coordinate the writes of both nodes.
- Write new code in the application that coordinates every write of both nodes to the shared volume at the block level.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to both instances.
- Format the shared volume with a clustered file system, and let the cluster software coordinate the writes of both nodes.

**Deciding phrases.** "same Availability Zone", "the same block storage", "does not coordinate writes", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** One zone and one shared block device decide this question. Multi-Attach gives each attached instance [full read and write permission](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) on one io2 volume. Standard file systems are not built for that, and the application does not order its own writes, so you [use a clustered file system](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system) and let the cluster software order them.

- Multi-Attach lets you [attach a single Provisioned IOPS SSD](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), as these two nodes are.
- With Multi-Attach you should [use a clustered file system](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system), which keeps the writes of both nodes safe.

**Why not.**

- "Create a General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume with ...": Multi-Attach is [supported exclusively on](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-only) io1 and io2 volumes, so a gp3 volume cannot serve both instances.
- "Format the shared volume with the XFS file ...": XFS is [not designed to be accessed simultaneously](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system) by several instances, so two nodes that mount it can corrupt the data.
- "Write new code in the application that coordinates ...": Code that [coordinates safe access at the application-level](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-multi-attach-application-requirements) can work, but it is new code to build and test.

**Twin.** If the stem said "web servers in three Availability Zones need the same files" instead: Amazon EFS, which stores data [within and across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing).

**Takeaway.** Shared block storage for a cluster in one zone means io2 with Multi-Attach and a clustered file system.

**Review.** [Multi-Attach shares one io2 volume and the application must coordinate writes](2-deep.md#multi-attach-shares-one-io2-volume-and-the-application-must-coordinate-writes-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q017 -->
### Question 15

A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The database uses two io2 Block Express data volumes with 12,000 provisioned IOPS each. The instance type supports at most 15,000 IOPS for Amazon EBS traffic. Monitoring shows that the database reaches about 15,000 IOPS in total. However, neither volume reaches its provisioned IOPS. The team must raise the I/O performance of the database. Which solution is the MOST operationally efficient way to meet this requirement?

- Raise the provisioned IOPS of both io2 Block Express volumes with Elastic Volumes, so that each volume has more IOPS than the database needs.
- Add a third io2 Block Express volume, and stripe the three volumes in a RAID 0 array so that their IOPS add up for the database.
- Move half of the data to a second instance of the same type with one of the volumes, and change the application to split its queries.
- Change the instance to a larger Nitro-based instance type whose EBS limit is higher than the total provisioned IOPS of both volumes.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Change the instance to a larger Nitro-based instance type whose EBS limit is higher than the total provisioned IOPS of both volumes.

**Deciding phrases.** "at most 15,000 IOPS for Amazon EBS traffic", "neither volume reaches its provisioned IOPS", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Why.** The total of about 15,000 IOPS, equal to the instance limit, decides this question. An instance's EBS performance is [bounded by the instance type's performance limits](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller) or by its volumes, [whichever is smaller](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller). Here the instance is the smaller limit, so a larger Nitro-based type raises the ceiling with no change to the volumes or the application.

**Why not.**

- "Raise the provisioned IOPS of both io2 Block ...": Performance is limited by the instance or the volumes, [whichever is smaller](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller), and the instance limit is already reached.
- "Add a third io2 Block Express volume, and ...": RAID 0 adds the IOPS of the volumes, but the total stays [bounded by the instance type's performance limits](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller).
- "Move half of the data to a second ...": It works, but a second instance and a change to the application take far more effort than one change of instance type.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the instance supports 40,000 IOPS, and each volume runs at its provisioned IOPS" instead: raise the provisioned IOPS of the volumes, because performance follows the instance or the volumes, [whichever is smaller](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller).

**Takeaway.** When an instance reaches its EBS limit, a larger instance type helps, and more volume IOPS do not.

**Review.** [The instance and its EBS bandwidth can cap a fast volume](2-deep.md#the-instance-and-its-ebs-bandwidth-can-cap-a-fast-volume-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q022 -->
### Question 16

A company stores financial records on Amazon EBS volumes in one AWS Region and takes a monthly snapshot of each volume. An auditor requires that each monthly snapshot is immutable for one year after the company creates it. Several administrators in the company's AWS account have full access to Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?

- Lock each monthly snapshot in governance mode for one year, with the lock set as soon as the company creates the snapshot.
- Create a Recycle Bin retention rule that keeps deleted EBS snapshots for 365 days, and restore any snapshot that someone deletes.
- Lock each monthly snapshot in compliance mode for one year, without a cooling-off period, as soon as the company creates the snapshot.
- Attach an IAM policy to every user and role that denies the ec2:DeleteSnapshot action on the monthly snapshots for one year.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Lock each monthly snapshot in compliance mode for one year, without a cooling-off period, as soon as the company creates the snapshot.

**Deciding phrases.** "immutable for one year", "administrators", "have full access to Amazon EC2", "MOST secure"

**Why.** Immutable means that the snapshot stays for the whole year, whatever permissions an administrator has. In compliance mode, [you can't unlock the snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode) after the cooling-off period, and [you can only increase the lock duration](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode). Governance mode, an IAM policy and a Recycle Bin rule each leave an administrator a way to delete the snapshot.

**Why not.**

- "Lock each monthly snapshot in governance mode for ...": It locks the snapshots, but in governance mode [users with appropriate IAM permissions can unlock](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-governance-mode) them, so an administrator can still remove the protection.
- "Create a Recycle Bin retention rule that keeps ...": Recycle Bin acts after a delete: a matching snapshot is [retained in the Recycle Bin](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-delete-retained-by-recycle-bin-rule), so users can still delete it, and it is not immutable.
- "Attach an IAM policy to every user and ...": Administrators with full access can edit or detach the policy and then delete a snapshot, while a locked snapshot is protected [regardless of their IAM permissions](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-no-user-can-delete).

**Twin.** If the stem said "a security team needs to remove a lock early after an approved review" instead: governance mode, because [users with appropriate IAM permissions can unlock](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-governance-mode) the snapshot.

**Takeaway.** Immutable snapshots, safe from administrators too: lock them in compliance mode.

**Review.** [Recycle Bin and snapshot lock stop snapshots from being deleted too early](2-deep.md#recycle-bin-and-snapshot-lock-stop-snapshots-from-being-deleted-too-early-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q019 -->
### Question 17

A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in two AWS Regions, us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Teams in both Regions create new Amazon EBS volumes every day with their own scripts and templates. A new security policy requires that every new EBS volume in these two Regions is encrypted at rest. The company does not want to change the scripts and templates of the teams. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 only, because the setting then applies to every Region of the account.
- Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 and in eu-west-1, and keep the AWS managed key of each Region as the default key.
- Run an AWS Lambda function every hour in each Region that finds unencrypted volumes and turns on encryption for each volume in place.
- Create a customer managed key in each Region, turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in both Regions, and set each new key as the default key.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 and in eu-west-1, and keep the AWS managed key of each Region as the default key.

**Deciding phrases.** "two AWS Regions", "every new EBS volume in these two Regions", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two Regions and the least effort decide this question. Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting), so you turn it on in each of the two Regions. After that, the account will [enforce the encryption of the new EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only) that the teams create there, and their scripts stay the same.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in ...": Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting), so new volumes in eu-west-1 stay unencrypted.
- "Run an AWS Lambda function every hour in ...": [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), so the function has no in-place step, and new volumes stay unencrypted between runs.
- "Create a customer managed key in each Region, ...": It works, but you then create and manage two keys, while EBS already has [a unique AWS managed key in each Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-aws-managed-key-alias-per-region).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the existing volumes must also be encrypted" instead: also replace each one from an encrypted snapshot copy, because encryption by default [has no effect on existing EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only).

**Takeaway.** Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting): turn it on in every Region where teams create volumes.

**Review.** [EBS encryption covers the volume its snapshots and the path to the instance](2-deep.md#ebs-encryption-covers-the-volume-its-snapshots-and-the-path-to-the-instance-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ebs-q021 -->
### Question 18

A company must keep one Amazon EBS snapshot of a database volume for each month for seven years to meet a compliance rule. The snapshots are kept for long-term storage and are infrequently accessed. When an audit needs an old snapshot, a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable. The company currently keeps all of these monthly snapshots in the standard tier. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to keep these snapshots?

- Keep the monthly snapshots in the standard tier, and add a tag to each snapshot that marks it as part of the compliance record.
- Copy the monthly snapshots into an Amazon S3 bucket through the Amazon S3 API, and store them in the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.
- Move each monthly snapshot to the Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive tier after it is created, and restore it from there for an audit.
- Delete every monthly snapshot except the most recent one, because the newest snapshot holds all of the data that the volume needs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Move each monthly snapshot to the Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive tier after it is created, and restore it from there for an audit.

**Deciding phrases.** "infrequently accessed", "a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Seven years of monthly snapshots that are rarely restored decide this question. AWS recommends the archive tier for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily), and its storage costs less than the standard tier. A restore from the archive tier can take [up to 72 hours](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours), which the three-day limit allows.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the monthly snapshots in the standard tier, ...": It meets the rule, but the archive tier offers [up to 75 percent lower snapshot storage costs](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-75-percent-lower-cost) for rarely accessed snapshots.
- "Copy the monthly snapshots into an Amazon S3 ...": EBS snapshots are [only available through the Amazon EC2 API](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-snapshots-not-via-s3-api), so the S3 API cannot copy them into a bucket.
- "Delete every monthly snapshot except the most recent ...": The newest snapshot restores the volume as it is today, and the compliance rule needs the state of each month.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an auditor needs a snapshot within one hour" instead: keep the snapshots in the standard tier, because an archive restore can take [up to 72 hours](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours).

**Takeaway.** Monthly snapshots kept for years and rarely restored belong in the EBS Snapshots Archive tier.

**Review.** [Data Lifecycle Manager and AWS Backup take snapshots on a schedule](2-deep.md#data-lifecycle-manager-and-aws-backup-take-snapshots-on-a-schedule-4-min)

</details>
